findings.paper_title: 13 Cabinet report - MTFP & Revenue Budget 2027-2030 - September 2026

findings.paper_title: 13 Cabinet report - MTFP & Revenue Budget 2027-2030 - September 2026
findings.headline: Government grant is being cut by £6.2m per annum in 2027/28 and 2028/29 as part of Fair Funding Review

findings.headline: Adult social care costs are the primary driver of budget deterioration, requiring additional provision in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council identifies adult social care cost increases in the current year as the main change from its February 2026 forecast. findings.matters: Unexpected demand-driven pressures in statutory services signal the council may face cost escalation beyond its control; this affects financial sustainability and reserve adequacy.

findings.paper_title: 13 Cabinet report - MTFP & Revenue Budget 2027-2030 - September 2026
findings.headline: Budget gap for next year has more than doubled to £12.0m, with a four-year gap of £40.5m
findings.detail: In February 2026, the council forecast a budget gap of £5.4m for 2027/28; by September 2026, this has increased to £12.0m. The four-year gap for 2027-2031 is now £40.5m, compared to £23m forecast for the preceding three-year period. This material deterioration in six months suggests emerging uncontrolled pressures or forecasting issues.
findings.matters: A budget gap that has doubled signals forecasting or control issues; lenders assess councils on their ability to live within their means, and this deterioration raises questions about financial management and reserves sustainability.
findings.quote: The budget gap for the four-year period 2027 to 2031 is £40.5m, and the gap for next year is £12.0m.

findings.paper_title: 12 Cabinet report - Budget Monitor 2026_27 - Month 4 Update vFinal
findings.headline: New spending controls escalating high-cost care placement approvals through director level to manage demand-driven overspends
findings.detail: In response to adult and children's social care overspends driven by placement costs, the council has introduced governance escalation requiring higher-cost placements to be approved by assistant director or director (depending on weekly cost threshold). The council is also implementing cost forecasting for all care decisions, detailed health-need assessment to shift costs to the ICB, and accelerated billing for service users with capital over £23,250. These measures are reactive controls to contain demand-driven overspends rather than addressing underlying cost or demand drivers.
findings.matters: Escalation controls are a sign the council is unable to manage demand within delegated approval frameworks and must intervene at director level. This slows placement decisions and signals the council expects continued high-cost placements. It does not solve the underlying cost-of-care or demographic demand problems.
findings.figures: Escalation threshold: placement cost-dependent (weekly cost determines level of approval required)
findings.quote: Additional controls are being implemented to escalate higher cost placements through the head of service and up to either the assistant director or director, depending on the expected weekly cost to ensure that a consistent approach is being recommended by practitioners.

findings.paper_title: 12 Cabinet report - Budget Monitor 2026_27 - Month 4 Update vFinal
findings.headline: Banwell bypass project risk status escalated to Red due to construction risks; Tropicana project remains Red due to funding shortfall
findings.detail: Two capital projects show deteriorating delivery. Banwell bypass moved from Amber to Red status after the project board received updates on construction risks escalated by the contractor; a further update will be shared with Cabinet. Tropicana (a Levelling Up Fund/Cultural Development Fund project) remains Red due to a funding shortfall and joint-funder complexity; the next board report is due November 2026. Capital programme spending is only 8% complete after four months.
findings.matters: Capital project delays and cost overruns tie up borrowing and reduce the council's capacity to deliver infrastructure. Contractor-escalated risks on Banwell bypass suggest scope or cost pressures. Tropicana's funding shortfall indicates external risks (funder conditions or match-funding requirements) are unresolved.

findings.paper_title: 12 Cabinet report - Budget Monitor 2026_27 - Month 4 Update vFinal
findings.headline: Approved savings plan delivering at only 91%, with £1.923m of mandated savings not forecast to materialize in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council approved £20.467m of savings for 2026/27 but now forecasts delivery of only £18.544m (91%). The £1.923m shortfall includes adult social care staffing savings being 'temporarily deferred' due to demand pressures and transformation programme delays. Because these savings form part of the approved budget, they cannot be removed without cabinet approval of replacement measures. This means the £1.923m remains a structural gap into future years.
findings.matters: Failed savings delivery is a leading indicator of structural overspend. The council's inability to achieve staffing reductions in adult care (the area with highest demand) and transformation savings shows planned efficiency gains are not materializing. This will pressure budgets in 2027/28 onwards.
findings.figures: Approved savings £20.467m; forecast delivery £18.544m (91%); shortfall £1.923m
findings.quote: The table shows that savings of £1.923m are currently not forecast or expected to be delivered this year although these items will remain within the base budget and will be delivered next year.

findings.paper_title: 12 Cabinet report - Budget Monitor 2026_27 - Month 4 Update vFinal
findings.headline: Medium-term structural deficit of £23m identified for years 2027/28–2029/30, increasing risk due to current year pressures
findings.detail: Beyond the 2026/27 in-year overspend, the council has identified a cumulative £23m budget gap over the following three years. This was flagged as 'at further risk because of the forecasts included within this report and the sharing of information by the government in terms of likely funding for local government in the coming years'. The council is updating its medium-term financial plan to address this.
findings.matters: A structural deficit signals the council's baseline spending is misaligned with available revenue and will require sustained service reductions, income rises, or borrowing. The worsening outlook suggests government funding pressures are accelerating.
findings.figures: Medium-term budget gap years 2027/28–2029/30: £23m
findings.quote: the council continued to reflect a £23m budget gap for the 3 years from 2027/28 onwards; that position continues to be at further risk because of the forecasts included within this report

findings.paper_title: 12 Cabinet report - Budget Monitor 2026_27 - Month 4 Update vFinal
findings.headline: General fund reserve of £10.6m represents only 4.41% of the net revenue budget, below the council's own tolerance given current financial risks
findings.detail: The council states this reserve is 'lower than the council would like given the scale of financial risks being managed'. With a £8.7m revenue overspend, £23m medium-term structural deficit, and £73m DSG liability only protected by a temporary override, the reserve provides less than 18 days of operational cover. The council is attempting to increase this but faces competing demands.
findings.matters: Low reserves reduce the council's resilience to shocks and force earlier intervention to borrowing or service cuts. With multiple material risks crystallizing simultaneously, the buffer is insufficient for a council in North Somerset's position.
findings.figures: Reserve balance £10.6m; reserve as % of net revenue budget 4.41%; net revenue budget £251.464m
findings.quote: The balance on this reserve is currently £10.6m which equates to just 4.41% of the net revenue budget, excluding town and parish council precepts. This is lower than the council would like given the scale of financial risks being managed

findings.paper_title: 12 Cabinet report - Budget Monitor 2026_27 - Month 4 Update vFinal
findings.headline: Adult social care overspending by £8.1m forecast due to demand-driven placement cost increases and income shortfalls
findings.detail: Adult services (30% of total budget) is forecast to overspend by £8.1m. The largest drivers are: £0.9m increase in transition costs for younger adults with higher complexity than budgeted; £2.4m increase in residential placements; £1.1m increase in supported living; £2.2m increase in home care and direct payments; £0.8m shortfall in S117 income from health where the ICB is not funding its share. The council has implemented in-year recovery measures including escalation thresholds for high-cost placements and tighter income collection, but the underlying demand pressure persists.
findings.matters: Adult social care is a statutory service with demand driven by demographics (the council has higher proportions of older people) and complexity. A £8.1m overspend in a £156m service (5.2%) shows the council is unable to contain costs even with investment added to the original budget. This signals structural demand pressure that will persist.
findings.figures: Adult services budget £156m; forecast overspend £8.1m; transition costs £0.9m overspend; residential placements £2.4m overspend; supported living £1.1m overspend; home care and direct payments £2.2m overspend; S117 income shortfall £0.8m
findings.quote: The net overspend for the directorate has reduced to £8.1m following the introduction of in-year recovery plan mitigations into the forecast.

findings.paper_title: 12 Cabinet report - Budget Monitor 2026_27 - Month 4 Update vFinal
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forecast to grow from £43m to £73m by year-end, with statutory protection ending March 2028
findings.detail: The DSG high needs block alone is forecast to overspend by £30m in 2026/27. The council's total DSG deficit, currently £43m, will likely reach £73m by year-end. Accounting rules currently allow this deficit to sit on the balance sheet under a temporary statutory override running until March 2028. If this ends, a £73m liability would exceed the council's entire general fund reserve of £10.6m. The government may fund up to 90% of the 2025/26 balance (estimated £38m) pending SEND reform approval, but future arrangements are unknown.
findings.matters: A £73m off-balance-sheet liability creates a structural solvency cliff unless government funding or reform materializes. The override expires in 21 months and the council has no funding solution for the balance. This is the single largest threat to the council's financial stability.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £43m (start of year); forecast £73m (year-end); high needs block overspend £30m; potential government grant £38m (90% of 2025/26 deficit); statutory override until March 2028
findings.quote: The council's DSG deficit was £43m at the beginning of the year and if the position remains unchanged, then it is likely to increase to £73m by the end of the year. Given that the general reserve balance is currently only £10.6m, it would not be sufficient to fund the deficit in its entirety should the statutory over-ride not be in place.

This £8.729m deficit is an improvement on the £11.809m reported in June, as directorates begin implementing recovery plans. The council states it can balance the budget through tighter spending controls, despite describing this as 'clearly challenging' and requiring 'decisive and collective actions'.
findings.matters: A £8.7m in-year deficit (3.47%) demonstrates significant financial pressure and questions whether recovery measures will hold. Lenders need confidence that the council can stabilize spending in volatile service areas.

findings.detail: The forecast outturn variance is £8.729m across the revenue budget. The council has released contingency budgets and is drawing down directorate risk reserves to offset this. The total reserve position shows transfers into the Dedicated Schools Deficit Reserve and other reserve movements that are now committed to managing current-year gaps rather than available for future shocks.
findings.matters: A 3.47% overspend on a full-year forecast (4 months into the year) suggests the 2026/27 financial position is structural, not one-off. Reserve drawdowns to manage current-year budgets reduce the council's financial resilience for 2027/28 and beyond.

A £29.9m deficit indicates the Top-up Funding budget (set at £12m revised, forecast £38.5m) is significantly misaligned with need. findings.paper_title: 10 CABINET DECISION - Highway Asset Management Strategy
findings.headline: Full DfT highway maintenance funding depends on maintaining compliance with asset management framework requirements
findings.detail: The council's eligibility for the maximum available DfT Highway Maintenance Block funding (including the Incentive element) depends on demonstrating asset management maturity. The paper explicitly states that 'Failure to maintain an appropriate strategic framework could therefore have financial implications for the Council through reduced funding opportunities, whilst also increasing the long-term risk of asset deterioration and higher whole-life maintenance costs.'
findings.matters: A substantial portion of highway maintenance funding comes from DfT, and loss of full eligibility would directly reduce the council's budget and increase long-term maintenance costs.
findings.figures: None quantified
findings.quote: Maintaining an up-to-date Highway Asset Management Framework that reflects recognised national guidance and best practice is an important element of demonstrating the Council's asset management maturity. This supports the Council in meeting Department for Transport requirements for highway maintenance funding and maintaining eligibility for the maximum available Highway Maintenance Block funding, including the Incentive element of the settlement.

findings.paper_title: 10 CABINET DECISION - Highway Asset Management Strategy
findings.headline: The council manages a £3.2 billion highway asset facing challenges from aging infrastructure, climate change and constrained public funding
findings.detail: North Somerset's highway network comprises over 1,100 kilometres of carriageways, footways, cycleways, bridges and drainage systems. The council identifies that meeting its statutory duty to maintain these assets 'has become increasingly challenging' due to aging infrastructure, climate change, customer expectations, inflation and funding constraints. The paper identifies 'High' current risk of asset deterioration and financial risk if not managed strategically.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can adequately maintain critical infrastructure and whether underfunding creates risk of deferred maintenance or asset deterioration.
findings.figures: approximately £3.2bn replacement value; over 1,100 kilometres of carriageways, footways and cycleways
findings.quote: Meeting this duty has become increasingly challenging due to ageing infrastructure, climate change, increased customer expectations, inflationary pressures and ongoing constraints on public sector funding.

findings.paper_title: 10.2 Appendix 2 - Highway Asset Management Strategy
findings.headline: Regional governance changes could materially alter transport funding arrangements and responsibilities for the council.
findings.detail: North Somerset is not currently part of the West of England Mayoral Combined Authority (WECA), but the strategy acknowledges that regional governance arrangements continue to evolve. The council has designed its strategy as a flexible framework to adapt to changes in national or regional funding, implying awareness that funding mechanisms may shift.
findings.matters: If WECA governance changes lead to different funding allocations or if transport responsibilities shift regionally, this could either improve or reduce the council's future funding available for highways, adding uncertainty to long-term financial planning.
findings.figures: Not currently part of WECA; four-year DfT settlement 2026/27–2029/30 provides stable short-term funding but regional arrangements remain uncertain
findings.quote: North Somerset is not currently part of the West of England Mayoral Combined Authority (WECA); however, regional governance arrangements continue to evolve, and future changes to how transport responsibilities and funding are organised remain possible.

findings.paper_title: 10.2 Appendix 2 - Highway Asset Management Strategy
findings.headline: Asset inventory data is incomplete for drainage, signage and street furniture, creating risk of underestimated future maintenance liabilities.
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that inventory completeness is essential for accurate lifecycle modelling and future cost forecasting, but current data gaps exist across drainage systems, street signage and street furniture. A targeted programme to improve these inventories is planned, but the council currently lacks complete data on major asset groups needed to forecast future maintenance needs accurately.
findings.matters: Incomplete asset data means the council's forecasts of future maintenance costs may be understated, creating unquantified liabilities. If full condition surveys later reveal greater deterioration or extent of assets than currently recorded, maintenance costs could spike unexpectedly.
findings.figures: 45,000 gullies with incomplete surveyed data; drainage, signage and street furniture identified as priority inventory improvement areas; structures data to be enhanced through improved GIS integration
findings.quote: Improving inventory completeness is essential for accurate lifecycle modelling, enabling the council to forecast future maintenance needs and optimise whole-life costs.

findings.paper_title: 10.2 Appendix 2 - Highway Asset Management Strategy
findings.headline: Climate change is accelerating asset deterioration, requiring increased investment in resilience that compounds the existing funding gap.
findings.detail: The council identifies coastal erosion and storm surges accelerating deterioration in Weston-super-Mare, Clevedon and Portishead; heavier rainfall and flash flooding increasing strain on drainage; and climate impacts accelerating wear on rural network infrastructure. Investment in resilience is embedded in the strategy but the document does not indicate additional funding has been secured for these climate-driven needs on top of existing maintenance demands.
findings.matters: Accelerating deterioration from climate impacts compounds the existing funding insufficiency. If assets are deteriorating faster due to climate, and funding is already insufficient for planned maintenance, the gap widens. This creates pressure for unplanned borrowing or service cuts.
findings.figures: Coastal areas experiencing accelerated deterioration; rural network showing increased vulnerability; 45,000 gullies requiring enhanced drainage investment for flood resilience
findings.quote: Coastal areas such as Weston-super-Mare, Clevedon and Portishead face accelerated deterioration from tidal flooding and storm surges, placing additional strain on carriageways, structures and drainage systems.

findings.paper_title: 10.2 Appendix 2 - Highway Asset Management Strategy
findings.headline: Available funding is insufficient to address all identified maintenance needs across the network.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that available DfT and transport capital funding cannot cover all maintenance requirements. The strategy acknowledges this structural gap and attempts to manage it through prioritisation processes that direct investment toward schemes delivering greatest benefit. This is an ongoing constraint, not a temporary funding dip.
findings.matters: A council unable to fund maintenance it deems necessary either defers spending (building future liabilities) or accepts degraded service and asset condition. For a lender, this signals long-term underfunding of a critical asset base and constrained borrowing capacity to fill the gap.
findings.figures: £3.2bn highway asset base; 699 miles of carriageway; 881 structures; 45,000 gullies in drainage system
findings.quote: Available funding is insufficient to address all identified maintenance needs across the highway network.
