findings.quote: The council's DSG deficit was over £26m at the beginning of the year and is likely to reach £41m by the end of the year... This grant will only be paid once each local authority has secured approval of their local area's Local SEND Reform Plan. Payments will be made from Autumn 2026 for local authorities whose local area plans are approved in the first round of assessment.

findings.paper_title: 11. Treasury Management Q3 2025-26 update report - Audit Committee
findings.headline: No new long-term borrowing raised in 2025/26 despite £178m capital spend
findings.detail: The council has raised no new external long-term borrowing by Q3 to fund its £178.1m capital programme, instead drawing on internal cash balances. Given the liability benchmark shows borrowing requirements rising to £108.5m by 2026/27, this position is not sustainable.
findings.matters: Using internal reserves to fund capital rather than borrowing defers but does not eliminate borrowing need; when borrowing becomes necessary, the council will lock in costs.
findings.figures: Zero new external long-term borrowing by 31 December 2025 against £178.1m capital expenditure forecast for 2025/26
findings.quote: No new external long-term borrowing had been undertaken by 31 December 2025, and none was taken during 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 11. Treasury Management Q3 2025-26 update report - Audit Committee
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast to reach £239.8m, requiring significant future borrowing
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement is growing from £189.3m in 2024/25 to £205.2m in 2025/26 to £239.8m by 2026/27. The liability benchmark indicates net loans requirement rising from £3.9m to £57.1m to £108.5m across the three years.
findings.matters: Growing CFR and rising liability benchmark show the council will need to significantly increase borrowing to fund its capital plans.
findings.figures: CFR £189.3m, £205.2m, £239.8m; liability benchmark £3.9m, £57.1m, £108.5m
findings.quote: The CFR is the council's underlying need to borrow for capital purposes; the latest forecast reflects current capital expenditure and financing assumptions.

findings.paper_title: 11. Treasury Management Q3 2025-26 update report - Audit Committee
findings.headline: Capital programme expanding rapidly to £230.9m by 2026/27
findings.detail: Planned capital expenditure is growing from £60.9m actual in 2024/25 to £178.1m forecast in 2025/26 and £230.9m estimated in 2026/27, with major spend on infrastructure, highways, transport, housing and SEND projects.
findings.matters: Rapid expansion of the capital programme materially increases the council's borrowing needs and future debt service obligations.
findings.quote: Capital expenditure at 31 December 2025 was £60.4m, with the largest areas of spend relating to major infrastructure projects, highways and transport schemes, housing-related projects and SEND / Safety Valve activity.

findings.paper_title: 11. Treasury Management Q3 2025-26 update report - Audit Committee
findings.headline: Budget spending pressures being masked by temporary investment income outperformance
findings.detail: Net interest income outperformed budget by £3m at Q3 with a further £1m improvement forecast, helping offset wider council spending pressures. This outperformance is due to higher cash balances and interest rates falling more slowly than expected—temporary factors that will reverse.
findings.matters: The council's underlying budget position is weaker than apparent; temporary investment income gains are masking structural spending pressures that will re-emerge.
findings.figures: £3m outperformance at Q3 plus £1m additional forecast; Bank Rate fell from 4.50% to 3.75%
findings.quote: Net interest income continued to outperform budget at Q3 by £3m helping offset wider in-year council spending pressures. This is as a result of higher cash balances (partly a result of capital programme rephasing) and interest rates falling at a slower pace than originally forecast.

findings.paper_title: 11. Treasury Management Q3 2025-26 update report - Audit Committee
findings.headline: Commercial property income loss due to major tenant departure
findings.detail: Commercial investment income is forecast below budget in 2025/26 due to loss of a major tenant. The impact is being managed through an earmarked smoothing reserve.
findings.matters: Loss of material property income is a specific revenue vulnerability; reliance on smoothing reserves signals planned use of buffers to absorb shocks.
findings.figures: Commercial investment income forecast below budget in 2025/26; impact managed through earmarked smoothing reserve
findings.quote: Commercial investment income is forecast to remain below budget in 2025/26, primarily because of the loss of a major tenant however, the impact on the revenue budget is being managed through the earmarked smoothing reserve.

findings.paper_title: 06.3 Cabinet - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 vFinal
findings.headline: Revenue reserves are falling from £42m to £24m over one year as the council finances capital spending from cash balances rather than external borrowing, depleting financial flexibility.
findings.detail: North Somerset is using internal borrowing (deploying reserves and investment balances to fund capital expenditure) to defer external borrowing costs. Internal borrowing is forecast to rise from £37.6m to £150.9m between 2025/26 and 2028/29. However, available revenue reserves are forecast to fall significantly from £42m to £24m in just one year, reducing the council's financial buffer for unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls.
findings.matters: Declining reserves limit the council's flexibility to handle unforeseen spending pressures or revenue shortfalls (e.g., from welfare or social care demand). It also signals that the council will transition from net investor to net borrower within the medium term, making it more sensitive to interest rate movements and refinancing risk.
findings.figures: Revenue reserves £42m (forecast 31/03/26) and £24m (forecast 31/03/27); internal borrowing £37.6m (2025/26) to £150.9m (2028/29); net investments currently £62.3m (£179.3m investments minus £117m borrowing)
findings.quote: The council's current strategy is to maintain borrowing and investments below their underlying levels, sometimes known as internal borrowing.

findings.paper_title: 06.3 Cabinet - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 vFinal
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement is growing 41% over three years, from £205m to £289m, while current external borrowing stands at only £117m, indicating substantial new borrowing will be needed.
findings.detail: North Somerset's underlying need to borrow for capital purposes is forecast to increase by £34.6m in 2026/27 alone and reach £289.3m by 2028/29. The council's capital investment program is particularly front-loaded, with spending of £230.9m planned for 2026/27 compared to £19.6m by 2028/29. This gap between the CFR and current borrowing means the council will need to access debt markets significantly.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that this council is entering a period of substantial capital expansion requiring significant new borrowing. The affordability depends on completing planned projects and achieving forecast capital receipts and grants. Interest rate sensitivity is high given the scale of new borrowing required.
findings.figures: CFR £205.2m (2025/26) rising to £239.8m (2026/27) and £289.3m (2028/29); current external borrowing £117.0m; capital investment £230.9m (2026/27)
findings.quote: The council's capital financing requirement (CFR) is expected to increase by £34.6m during 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 06.3 Cabinet - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 vFinal
findings.headline: Council is switching debt repayment calculation from straight-line to annuity method, reducing annual MRP charges by £1.667m immediately and claiming £30m savings over ten years.
findings.detail: North Somerset is adopting an annuity-based Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) method from April 2025, which spreads debt repayment costs more evenly across asset lives. This reduces the 2025/26 MRP charge from £9.9m to £8.233m. The change is financially beneficial short-term but extends the period over which principal is repaid and slightly increases total interest costs.
findings.matters: Lower annual MRP charges reduce the revenue cost of capital borrowing, easing budget pressure and improving cash flow in the short term. However, a lender would want to verify that asset useful lives are correctly estimated, as the annuity method is sensitive to these assumptions.
findings.figures: MRP saving of £1,667k in 2025/26; claimed savings of up to £30m over next 10 years; Pre-2008 borrowing saving £370k, Post-2008 borrowing saving £1,297k
findings.quote: By using the PWLB certainty rate available on the 1st April 2025 for the 2025/26 financial year in the annuity calculations, the council can achieve both short-term and long-term savings, of up to £30 million over the next 10 years.

findings.paper_title: 06.1 Capital Strategy 2026_2030 vFinal
findings.headline: Capital spending severely constrained by revenue budget pressures; S151 officer restricting new investment unless externally funded or reprioritised
findings.detail: The CFO explicitly notes that new capital spending is being limited in the short-term unless proposals come with external funding, strong business cases, or involve reprioritisation of existing schemes. This constraint reflects 'ongoing work to assess the condition of the council's asset base, underlying risks associated with capital investment plans, pressures within other areas of the council's finances and lack of available capital resources'. Only one council-funded scheme (Carlton Street) has been approved for 2026/27, indicating tight capital resource discipline.
findings.matters: Reveals constrained borrowing headroom despite £99m (21%) of £461.759m programme financed by borrowing; limits council's ability to respond to emerging capital needs; signals revenue budget stress translating to capital constraints
findings.figures: Only £2.75m council-funded capital approved for 2026/27; £99m total borrowing requirement from current programme
findings.quote: the approach supported by the S151 Officer in respect of capital spending in the short-term, is that it must be to limit new areas of spending unless the proposals come with external funding, are supported by a business case or can be re-prioritised by removing something from the existing programme.

findings.paper_title: 06.1 Capital Strategy 2026_2030 vFinal
findings.headline: Voyage Learning Campus secondary site replacement of £16-17m required to meet statutory SEND provision, currently in business case development
findings.detail: The council's current Voyage Learning Campus (secondary alternative provision school) is located on a leased industrial estate and no longer fits service requirements. Replacement facility at Locking Head Drove is estimated at £16-17m and being developed for Council consideration in spring 2026. The council explicitly states failure to deliver would force statutory SEND placements at 'more costly independent schools elsewhere', creating cost escalation exposure if the capital scheme is delayed or underfunded.
findings.matters: Statutory obligation with no discretion; service failure risk creates cost escalation through costly out-of-area placements; scheme still in feasibility phase with costs being validated
findings.figures: £16-17m estimated cost (costs being validated); funding from S106, High Needs capital grant, basic need grants
findings.quote: A failure to have a site for these young people children would mean that NSC would risk not fulfilling its statutory duty as places would need to be secured at more costly independent schools elsewhere in the county.

findings.paper_title: 06.1 Capital Strategy 2026_2030 vFinal
findings.headline: VERY HIGH strategic risk that council cannot balance revenue budget or deliver statutory services within available resources
findings.detail: The Strategic Risk Register identifies a VERY HIGH residual risk that the council may be unable to deliver statutory services within available resources, explicitly noting the council may not be able to balance the budget in the current financial year or set and approve a balanced budget in future years. This is coupled with a HIGH risk of being unable to deliver capital projects within approved budgets due to cost inflation and governance issues. The council notes 'many uncertainties and outstanding workstreams' affecting this assessment.
findings.matters: Explicit council-identified risk to financial sustainability and service delivery; impacts medium-term borrowing capacity and ratios; suggests structural deficit issues
findings.figures: VERY HIGH and HIGH residual risk ratings in Strategic Risk Register
findings.quote: This could potentially be the position if the council is unable to resolve its financial difficulties in the current year meaning that it may not be able to balance the budget in the current year and set and approve a balanced budget in future years.

findings.paper_title: 06.1 Capital Strategy 2026_2030 vFinal
findings.headline: £168m capital re-profiled from 2025/26 into future years, raising delivery forecasting concerns
findings.detail: The council has reduced the 2025/26 capital budget by £168m through re-profiling activity, moving this spending to later years. Most changes relate to major schemes (each approved with indicative profiles later updated with detailed delivery plans). The council reports 30% year-to-date spend but notes this figure would be significantly lower without the re-profiling, raising concerns about forecasting accuracy and delivery capability.
findings.matters: Indicates systematic forecasting risk on major schemes; 30% spend rate dependent on moving targets rather than actual delivery suggests contingency adequacy issues
findings.figures: £168m re-profiled; £53.381m spent year-to-date; £158.527m committed; 30% reported spend rate
findings.quote: The budget for the current financial year has been reduced by £168m due to re-profiling activity, and this sum has been moved into later years. This means that whilst the council is now reporting actual spend to date of 30% for the year, this proportion would have been much lower without the changes and could be seen as a cause for concern in terms of the council being able to effectively plan its' finances.

findings.paper_title: 06.1 Capital Strategy 2026_2030 vFinal
findings.headline: Carlton Street car park upper floors closed due to health and safety concerns, requiring £2.75m remediation and service-funded borrowing
findings.detail: The upper floors of Carlton Street car park in Weston remain closed pending structural assessment. The closure reduces council parking income and service availability. A capital project is being added to remediate structural issues, replace lifts and lighting, and address water ingress, estimated at £2.75m and funded through service-funded borrowing, pending further due diligence on scope and cost.
findings.matters: Material asset impairment affecting both service provision and revenue; unplanned capital requirement adds to borrowing burden during period of revenue constraint
findings.figures: £2.75m estimated project cost; upper floors currently non-operational
findings.quote: the upper floors of the car park are currently closed due to health and safety related concerns whilst engineering and structural assessments are being made. These closures not only affect residents and visitors who would like to be able to use the car park but they also impact on the council financially because less income is being received.

findings.paper_title: 05 7 Council tax setting Report - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 - original draft vFinal (1)
findings.headline: Low council tax base explicitly identified as structural income constraint preventing council from raising revenues needed for statutory services.
findings.detail: The council states in justifying the exceptional government support request: 'Although we have made savings elsewhere within the budget, our low taxbase means that we have not been able to generate the income we need to deliver services to our residents.' This is a structural disadvantage that cannot be remedied by local action and limits the council's ability to self-fund service delivery.
findings.matters: A structural disadvantage in the tax base means the council is disproportionately dependent on government funding and cannot easily raise own revenue to offset funding reductions, limiting financial flexibility and creating long-term vulnerability.
findings.figures: Low taxbase explicitly constraining income generation
findings.quote: Members will be aware that North Somerset Council made a request for council tax flexibility for next year because it is facing financial difficulties, the cost and demand for social care services has risen by more than our funding for the last few years and although we have made savings elsewhere within the budget, our low taxbase means that we have not been able to generate the income we need to deliver services to our residents.

findings.paper_title: 05 7 Council tax setting Report - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 - original draft vFinal (1)
findings.headline: Adult social care provider fees uplifted below National Living Wage growth (3% vs 4.1%), with providers asked to make efficiency savings.
findings.detail: The council is uplifting adult social care provider fees at 3% for most services (nursing, residential, domiciliary care, supported living, extra care, reablement) against a National Living Wage increase of 4.1%. The paper states 'the council's plans include asking providers to make their own efficiency savings meaning that the uplifts applied will be slightly lower than the headline rate.' This occurs against £130m+ annual spending with providers.
findings.matters: Fees rising below NLW while asking providers for efficiency savings creates significant market sustainability risk; providers may withdraw services, reduce quality, or become financially unstable, disrupting care provision and potentially creating contingent council liabilities.
findings.figures: Provider uplifts: 3% for most services (nursing, residential, domiciliary, supported living, extra care, reablement); NLW at 4.1%; council spends £130m+ on provider payments
findings.quote: Given that the council currently spends over £130m on payments to providers, the impact of these proposals will be significant. Whilst the council has a statutory duty under the Care Act 2014 to maintain market sustainability by uplifting costs paid to providers, this needs to be balanced against affordability. Given the overall financial position, the council's draft budget for next year includes a range of savings proposals linked to introducing efficiencies and transforming in-house services and so this approach is also being considered for services we buy in. As such, the council's plans include asking providers to make their own efficiency savings.

findings.paper_title: 05 7 Council tax setting Report - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 - original draft vFinal (1)
findings.headline: Persistent unmet demand escalation in children in care and SEND, with council continually re-basing budgets upward yet still overspending.
findings.detail: The council notes that 'As in previous years, account has been taken of current and future demand and once again additional provision has been built into the recommended budget for these areas in 2026/27.' This pattern of repeated re-basing suggests the council is chasing demand rather than controlling it. The paper identifies children in care and SEND as areas of 'most notable changes' where demand growth continues to outpace budget increases.
findings.matters: Uncontrollable statutory demand in children's and special education services is a key structural budget pressure; the council's inability to manage demand despite repeated budget uplifts suggests ongoing deficits in these areas are inevitable without external intervention.
findings.figures: Continued additional provision built into 2026/27 for children in care and SEND
findings.quote: The most notable changes have arisen in areas such as children in care and those with special educational needs and disabilities, as well as increases in care needs for older and vulnerable adults. As in previous years, account has been taken of current and future demand and once again additional provision has been built into the recommended budget for these areas in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 05 7 Council tax setting Report - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 - original draft vFinal (1)
findings.headline: General Fund Balance falling to 4.44% of budget; £27.09m (23%) reduction in total reserves forecast by end 2025/26.
findings.detail: The council's General Fund Balance is projected at £10.47m (4.44% of the £240.426m net budget), within the 4-6% target range but at the lower end. Total earmarked and general reserves are forecast to fall by £27.09m or 23% by end of 2025/26. The CIPFA financial resilience report explicitly recommended the council 'give more focus on re-building reserve balances to support future financial resilience.'
findings.matters: Reserves provide the only cushion for unexpected costs, demand spikes, or funding shortfalls; a 23% reduction combined with ongoing uncertainty leaves limited buffer for shocks, and CIPFA's recommendation to rebuild indicates external concern.
findings.figures: £10.47m General Fund Balance (4.44% of budget); £27.09m reduction in total reserves (23% decline)
findings.quote: There is a forecast reduction of £27.09m, or 23% by the end of 2025/26 although most of the draw downs in year are to support planned investments, events and strategies. The Cipfa resilience report did highlight the need for the council to give more focus on re-building reserve balances to support future financial resilience.

findings.paper_title: 05 7 Council tax setting Report - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 - original draft vFinal (1)
findings.headline: Government funding to reduce by 20% (£18.6m) over the 2026-2029 period due to Fair Funding Review.
findings.detail: The 3-year government settlement covering 2026-2029 includes major changes through the Fair Funding Review that will reduce North Somerset's government funding by £18.6m (20%) over three years. The Section 151 Officer states this 'presents a further risk to our goal of achieving long-term financial sustainability.' Notably, the settlement was only released in late December 2025 with additional details in February 2026, giving limited planning time.
findings.matters: A 20% reduction in government funding over three years represents a major long-term headwind that will require either further service reduction, tax rises, or reserve drawdown, and limits the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £18.6m reduction over 3 years (2026-2029); represents 20% cut to government funding
findings.quote: the 3-year settlement which covers the period 2026 to 2029 also included significant changes brought about by the Fair Funding Review, the most significant of which will be a reduction of £18.6m, or 20% in government funding over the next three years.

findings.paper_title: 05 7 Council tax setting Report - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 - original draft vFinal (1)
findings.headline: Council committed to £60m savings over 5 years (£20m next year) with acknowledged risk if delivery plans fail.
findings.detail: The council has developed a £60m savings programme across 2025-2030 to manage ongoing demand and cost growth, with £20m targeted for delivery in 2026/27 alone. The Section 151 Officer explicitly notes that 'Savings of this scale do represent a risk if they are not supported by clear delivery plans' and that efforts have been made to embed clear delivery plans before each financial year.
findings.matters: A £60m savings programme represents a substantial structural transformation over 5 years; failure to deliver even a portion creates immediate new funding gaps that would likely need to be covered by reserves or further tax rises.
findings.quote: The rising cost base has resulted in the council developing savings proposals of almost £60m over the period 2025 to 2030, with £20m of this planned for delivery next year. Savings of this scale do represent a risk if they are not supported by clear delivery plans and so efforts have been made to look ahead across all years of the Plan and ensure that these are in place before the start of each financial year.

findings.paper_title: 05 7 Council tax setting Report - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 - original draft vFinal (1)
findings.headline: Draft budget in February showed £8.4m unbalanced gap that required exceptional government support and major savings to close.
findings.detail: The Cabinet's draft revenue budget in February 2026 totalled £236.417m but was not fully financed by available resources, resulting in an £8.4m budget gap with no immediate solution. This gap was closed only through the exceptional 4% council tax flexibility plus £2.7m of new savings proposals.
findings.matters: A £8.4m gap (3.5% of budget) unable to be closed through routine measures indicates serious structural budget imbalance and dependency on government discretion.
findings.figures: £8.4m budget gap; draft budget £236.417m
findings.quote: The draft net revenue budget, excluding the town and parish council precepts, totalled £236.417m at that time, although was not fully financed by resources meaning that the Cabinet were unable to present a balanced budget for the forthcoming financial year. A budget gap of £8.4m was reported at the meeting.

findings.paper_title: 05 7 Council tax setting Report - Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026-27 - original draft vFinal (1)
findings.headline: Granted exceptional 4% council tax flexibility as 1 of only 7 councils nationally, signalling severe financial distress.
findings.detail: The government approved only 7 councils for extraordinary council tax flexibility above standard capping limits. North Somerset received 4% flexibility (on top of 2.99% standard limit plus 2% ASC precept), enabling an 8.99% total increase for 2026/27. This flexibility generates £5.977m of additional income and became part of the base budget solution.
findings.matters: Being 1 of 7 councils nationally to receive exceptional financial support is a stark indicator the council is in financial distress and the government views it as at risk.
findings.figures: 4% flexibility; 8.99% total increase (2.99% + 4% + 2%); £5.977m additional income
findings.quote: North Somerset Council was given council tax flexibility of 4% which means that it can approve a general council tax increase of 6.99% (i.e. 2.99% plus 4%) as well as increase tax by 2% through the Adult Social Care precept. In total, this provides flexibility to increase council tax by 8.99%, for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 9. External Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Journal control deficiency: mandatory approval for high-value journals not yet implemented at system level
findings.detail: Auditors identified that journal approval controls remain manual (using Excel templates) despite a prior year recommendation to implement system-based controls. Management agreed to a compromise: mandatory secondary approval for journals exceeding £2.5m. Testing found one journal over this threshold that bypassed the control; management classified this as trivial. The control deficiency persists after two audit cycles.
findings.matters: Manual journal controls are a known weakness in preventing unauthorised transactions and errors. The fact that control bypasses continue to occur (even if classified as trivial) and system-level controls remain unimplemented suggests management override risk is not adequately mitigated.
findings.figures: £2.5m threshold for mandatory approval; 141,303 transactions posted to ledger in year, 4,992 were manual postings from 60 different user IDs
findings.quote: One journal selected for testing was not reviewed or approved via the journals template due to the trivial nature of the journal. Management have agreed to implement a mandatory secondary approval for any journals that exceed value of £2.5m.

findings.paper_title: 9. External Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report 2024-25
findings.headline: NHS pooled budget agreements remain unsigned for second consecutive year, creating unsupported disclosures
findings.detail: S75 and S256 agreements between North Somerset Council and NHS BNSSG ICB have not been signed by either party and remain in draft status. This is identical to the prior year finding, indicating no resolution has been achieved. While auditors were able to gain assurance from other sources, the unsigned agreements mean accounting entries and disclosures lack legal documentation support.
findings.matters: Unsigned agreements indicate governance friction with NHS partners and create audit risk around unsubstantiated disclosures. For lenders, it suggests coordination challenges with integrated care systems and uncertainty around pooled budget commitments.
findings.figures: Agreements remain unsigned as of audit date (27 November 2025)
findings.quote: S75 and S256 agreements between the Council and NHS BNSSG ICB have not been signed by either party. The Council have not [...]... Similar to the prior year, s75 and s256 remained unsigned and in draft status.

findings.paper_title: 9. External Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Land and building valuations lack year-end assurance methodology, a recurring control gap
findings.detail: The council's £64.6 million land and building portfolio is valued on a rolling 5-year cycle (36% revalued in 2024-25). Auditors identified that the valuer provides valuations as at 1 January but does not confirm these remain fair value at 31 March year-end. While management undertakes its own indexation, auditors recommend the valuer should also review potential movements. This is a control weakness that has been recommended to management for two audit cycles.
findings.matters: Land and buildings represent 30% of the council's balance sheet. A methodology gap between valuation date and reporting date creates a window of potential material misstatement that increases audit risk and suggests governance weakness in asset management.
findings.figures: £64.647 million (land and buildings at 31 March 2025); 36% of portfolio revalued during the year
findings.quote: The valuer does not provide this assurance and have raised a recommendation point for this. While management do undertake their own indexation exercise to provide this assurance, the risk of misstatement is not fully mitigated until the valuer also reviews the potential movements.

findings.paper_title: 9. External Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Significant uncertainties identified in investment property valuations totalling £53.5 million
findings.detail: The council holds investment properties valued at £53.5 million, including the North Worle District Centre and Sovereign Centre in Weston-Super-Mare. Prior year audit work identified material errors: land area measurement uncertainty (£403.5k extrapolated) and rounding issues (£122.7k extrapolated). Current year audit work remains ongoing on these valuations, though no material issues noted to date. These assets are critical to the council's financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Investment property forms the council's commercial portfolio and directly impacts balance sheet strength and borrowing capacity. Identified valuation uncertainties and prior errors suggest governance gaps in how these material assets are measured and controlled.
findings.figures: £53.512 million (2025) vs £44.894 million (2024); increase of £8.618 million. Prior year extrapolated errors: £403.5k + £122.7k
findings.quote: The Council's commercial investment portfolio consists of the North Worle District Centre and the Sovereign Centre in Weston-Super-Mare... total year end valuation of investment properties was £53.512 million, a net increase of £8.618 million from 2023/24

findings.paper_title: 9. External Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Net pension liability decreased by £35.7 million to £40.8 million
findings.detail: The Authority's net pension liability improved significantly from £76.5 million in 2023-24 to £40.8 million at 31 March 2025. The auditor's work on pension valuations found no significant issues with the actuary, assumptions or methodology. The improvement reflects favourable market movements and updated actuarial assumptions (discount rate 5.80%, pension increase rate 2.7%).
findings.matters: A significant improvement in pension liability strengthens the balance sheet and reduces future obligations; this is material for both lender risk assessment and the council's financial flexibility for other commitments.
findings.figures: £40.821 million (2025) vs £76.499 million (2024); decrease of £35.7 million
findings.quote: The Authority's net pension liability at 31 March 2025 is £40.821 million (2023/24: £76.499 million)... There has been a decrease of £35.7 million in the net actuarial deficit during 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: 9. External Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Auditor not satisfied that the council has proper arrangements for securing financial sustainability
findings.detail: Grant Thornton has identified two significant weaknesses in the Authority's arrangements and has explicitly concluded they are not satisfied that the council has proper arrangements for securing financial sustainability. This is a qualified Value for Money assessment, with detailed findings set out in the accompanying Auditor's Annual Report. This matters because it signals to the auditor (an independent qualified firm) that the council's approach to financial planning and sustainability is inadequate.
findings.matters: Lenders assess borrowing councils on financial sustainability; an auditor's conclusion that arrangements are inadequate is a material risk indicator for lending decisions and council finances officers need to understand and address these weaknesses.
findings.figures: Two significant weaknesses identified
findings.quote: We identified two significant weaknesses in the Authority's arrangements and are not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for securing financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: 10. External Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Auditor raised two Key Recommendations (significant weaknesses) on DSG deficit action and recurrent savings delivery, continuing a pattern of unresolved prior-year recommendations.
findings.detail: The same DSG deficit recommendation was raised in 2023/24 and re-raised in 2024/25, with auditor noting 'Limited progress made' and stating 'Proper arrangements were not in place to address the DSG deficit in 2024/25.' This signals the council has not successfully implemented solutions, raising questions about management capacity or strategic focus. The savings gap recommendation is new but reflects the widening structural problem.
findings.matters: Unresolved auditor recommendations, especially when re-raised, indicate either management capacity constraints or governance weakness. A lender should assess whether the council has the leadership and resources to deliver on commitments.
findings.figures: KR1 raised 2023/24, re-raised 2024/25; KR2 new in 2024/25
findings.quote: Prior Recommendation Raised 2023/24... The DSG deficit continued to increase in 2024/25, with an in-year overspend of £12.7m... Proper arrangements were not in place to address the DSG deficit in 2024/25. Limited progress made.

findings.paper_title: 10. External Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: System fragmentation in Children's Services limits procurement visibility and creates risk of non-compliance: spend is spread across three unintegrated systems (Agresso, Contract register, LCS) with no clear ownership.
findings.detail: Agresso (finance), Contract (register), and LCS (case management) are not integrated, limiting visibility into placements and packages managed outside traditional procurement channels. Procurement's oversight is limited, particularly of high-risk care-related spend. This has been raised as an improvement recommendation (IR3), but without integration, compliance risks persist.
findings.matters: System fragmentation and poor spend visibility increases fraud, compliance, and value-for-money risks. A lender would be concerned that the council cannot accurately track or control spending in its most volatile and expensive service area.
findings.figures: Three unintegrated systems; limited visibility into Children's Services spend
findings.quote: There is limited visibility into contract-related spend within Children's Services due to fragmented systems and lack of integration between Agresso (finance), Contract (contract register), and LCS (case management).

findings.paper_title: 10. External Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Adult Services overspent by £8.7m in 2024/25, with 2025/26 budget including a £15.5m increase due to ongoing demand pressures and demographic change.
findings.detail: Adult Social Care, alongside Children's Services, is a key driver of budget pressure. The council allocated significant new funding (£15.5m increase) in 2025/26 to cover demand, but forecasting accuracy remains a concern. Unlike Children's, Adult Services has shown some improvement through transformation programmes and Power BI dashboards, but the scale of increase suggests persistent structural demand.
findings.matters: Adult Services is a statutory, demand-led service. Rising costs signal either demographic pressure the council cannot control or service redesign that is not delivering savings. Either way, a lender should understand whether the council has a realistic plan to manage this spending trajectory.
findings.figures: £8.7m Adult Services overspend in 2024/25; £15.5m budget increase for 2025/26
findings.quote: The council's 2025/26 budget includes over £30 million in increased spending compared to the 2024/25 MTFP budget. With inflation, changes and re-basing leading to a £15.5m increase allocated to adult social care and £16.2m to children's services due to ongoing pressures.

findings.paper_title: 10. External Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: The council is considering application for Exceptional Financial Support from the government due to severe financial pressures, with a decision expected December 2025 or January 2026.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton notes that 'Application for Exceptional Financial Support, a mechanism used by the UK Government to provide financial assistance to local authorities that are experiencing severe financial pressures and are unable to balance their budgets without additional support, is now a serious consideration for the Council.' No decision is expected until December 2025 or January 2026. This signals the council may be unable to balance its medium-term financial plan without government intervention.
findings.matters: Exceptional Financial Support is a marker of acute financial distress. A council in receipt of it is under formal government oversight and facing service restrictions or loan repayment conditions. A lender would treat this as a material increase in counterparty risk.
findings.figures: Decision expected December 2025 / January 2026
findings.quote: Application for Exceptional Financial Support, a mechanism used by the UK Government to provide financial assistance to local authorities that are experiencing severe financial pressures and are unable to balance their budgets without additional support, is now a serious consideration for the Council.

findings.paper_title: 10. External Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Children's Services placements are vastly underbudgeted: the 2024/25 budget allocated for 11 residential placements against actual demand of 30–40, contributing to an £16.8m overspend.
findings.detail: The number of children in care has risen from approximately 200 pre-pandemic to 270, driven by increased complexity, unaccompanied asylum-seeking children, and high-cost unregistered placements. The 2024/25 budget significantly underestimated placement demand, creating a structural gap that forecasting tools and leadership turnover had not corrected. Despite external support (Impower) and improved modelling, demand remains volatile and worst-case scenarios often exceed what is affordable within the MTFP.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether a council has visibility and control of its highest-cost, most volatile service. A £16m overspend driven by a 3–4x underestimate of placement numbers signals poor forecasting capability and structural budget risk that could persist or worsen.
findings.figures: Budget allocated for 11 residential placements vs actual need 30–40; children in care risen from ~200 pre-pandemic to ~270; £16.8m Children's Services overspend in 2024/25; 2025/26 includes £16.2m increase for Children's pressures
findings.quote: The 2024/25 budget significantly underestimated demand, allocating for just 11 residential placements against actual need of 30–40.

findings.paper_title: 10. External Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Reserve depletion is accelerating, with useable reserves forecast to fall from £116.3m (2024/25) to just over £40m by 2027/28, reducing financial headroom materially.
findings.detail: The council drew down £12.8m from earmarked reserves in 2024/25 (nearly £5m for Children's Services alone) to manage service pressures and avoid Exceptional Financial Support. Total useable reserves have fallen from £125.8m in 2023/24 to £116.3m in 2024/25 and are forecast to drop to just over £40m by 2027/28. Grant Thornton notes this reflects 'the fragility of the Council's financial resilience' and recommends a structured multi-year replenishment plan.
findings.matters: Declining reserves limit the council's ability to absorb demand volatility, service failures, or external shocks. A lender would be concerned about a council with less than three months of operating costs in reserves by 2027/28, with no clear plan to replenish them.
findings.figures: £12.8m earmarked reserve drawdown in 2024/25; useable reserves fell from £125.8m to £116.3m; forecast to fall to just over £40m by end 2027/28
findings.quote: The CIPFA Financial Resilience Review (June 2025) recommends the need for a structured, multi-year replenishment plan and clearer reserve categorisation to improve transparency and strategic alignment.

findings.paper_title: 10. External Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: The medium-term savings gap has widened to £46m over five years, with many current savings plans relying on non-recurrent measures rather than embedded efficiencies.
findings.detail: The savings gap expanded from £10m over three years to £46m over five years. The council achieved a balanced 2024/25 budget through £15m in reserve drawdowns and contingency releases alongside non-recurrent savings. For 2025/26, the council is again using £9.1m of one-off reserves to balance the budget. The auditor identifies this as unsustainable and rates it a significant weakness in financial sustainability.
findings.matters: A lender assessing sustainability needs to know whether budget balance is real or reliant on temporary measures. Non-recurrent savings and reserve use cannot continue indefinitely; the council risks being unable to close its gap without material service reductions or exceptional support.
findings.figures: Savings gap widened from £10m over 3 years to £46m over 5 years; £9.1m one-off reserves used to balance 2025/26 budget
findings.quote: The savings gap has widened from £10m over three years, as at when our review began in August 2025, to £46m over the next five years.

findings.paper_title: 10. External Auditors Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has deteriorated sharply, reaching £26m cumulative with £12.7m overspend in 2024/25 alone, and the statutory override protecting it ends in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The DSG in-year overspend nearly quadrupled from £3.6m in 2023/24 to £12.7m in 2024/25, increasing the cumulative deficit to £26m. The statutory override allowing councils to exclude SEND-related deficits from the general fund ends in 2027/28, after which the council must absorb the deficit. Without a realistic savings trajectory agreed with the Department for Education under the Safety Valve programme, this presents a material and unresolved financial risk.
findings.matters: Once the statutory override expires, the council will have to absorb a £26m+ deficit into its general fund, which could significantly deplete reserves and severely constrain the council's ability to respond to other financial shocks or service pressures.
findings.figures: £12.7m in-year overspend 2024/25 (up from £3.6m in 2023/24); cumulative deficit £26m; statutory override ends 2027/28
findings.quote: The DSG position has worsened, with a £12.7m in-year overspend in 2024/25 (£3.6m in 2023/24); increasing the cumulative deficit to £26m.

findings.paper_title: 11. TM Outturn report 2024-25 and 2025-26 Q1 update
findings.headline: £4.2m investment income windfall masking revenue pressures; unsustainable with falling rates
findings.detail: Investment income exceeded budget by £4.2m in 2024/25 and was used to offset service spending pressures. This windfall is unsustainable: Bank Rate fell to 4.25% and 2025/26 forecasts £7.2m income versus £10.6m achieved in 2024/25. Declining rates remove this one-off support for the revenue budget.
findings.matters: Use of investment windfall to offset service pressures signals structural budget strain; declining rates remove this relief, exposing council to difficult cuts or alternative funding solutions
findings.figures: 2024/25: net interest income actual £10.6m vs budget £6.4m (variance £4.2m); 2025/26 forecast £7.2m (£3.4m reduction); Bank Rate fell from 4.5% to 4.25% (May 2025)
findings.quote: despite the bank base rate falling during 2024/25, net interest income earned on all investments exceeded the budget by £4.2m, this was used to offset in year spending pressures in other areas

findings.paper_title: 11. TM Outturn report 2024-25 and 2025-26 Q1 update
findings.headline: Liability benchmark forecast to rise sharply; borrowing strategy carries elevated risk
findings.detail: Liability benchmark (prudent minimum borrowing) forecast rises from £3.9m actual (2024/25) to £82.7m (2025/26) to £121.3m (2026/27). The treasury report explicitly warns that borrowing significantly above this benchmark carries higher risk—flagging that the capital financing strategy exceeds prudent parameters.
findings.matters: Liability benchmark is the standard measure of prudent borrowing for councils; forecasting much higher borrowing indicates elevated risk in the capital strategy and questions whether plans are fully sustainable
findings.figures: Liability benchmark £3.9m (2024/25) vs £82.7m forecast (2025/26) vs £121.3m forecast (2026/27); 30x increase over three years
findings.quote: This benchmark is currently £3.9m and is forecast to rise to £121.3m over the next three years. Whilst borrowing may be above the liability benchmark, strategies involving borrowing which is significantly above the liability benchmark carry higher risk.

findings.paper_title: 11. TM Outturn report 2024-25 and 2025-26 Q1 update
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement rising £41.5m in one year; £287m capital programme
findings.detail: Capital financing requirement rises 22% from £189.3m (2024/25) to £230.9m (2025/26) to £252.7m (2026/27). The £287.4m capital programme for 2025/26 is a 5-fold increase from £60.9m actual spending in 2024/25, though the council acknowledges this forecast will be updated and reprofiled.
findings.matters: Rapid CFR growth indicates expanding long-term debt obligations and debt service costs; £287m annual capital programme is unusually large and represents significant new financial commitments that must be serviced
findings.quote: The CFR is expected to increase by £41.5m during 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 11. TM Outturn report 2024-25 and 2025-26 Q1 update
findings.headline: £0.247m loss on UBS pooled fund; forced seller position
findings.detail: UBS closed a pooled fund while the council's £1m investment was below its purchase price, forcing a realised loss of £0.247m. Though mitigated by smoothing reserve, this demonstrates that pooled fund investments—typically considered lower-risk—can crystallise material losses when funds close at unfavourable times.
findings.matters: Realised losses on pooled investments erode capital; forced seller position illustrates vulnerability to fund closures; smoothing reserve requirement indicates recognition of significant investment risk
findings.figures: £1m investment, £0.247m loss realised, £0.314m interest received over ~8 years; net yield £0.067m
findings.quote: The council became a "forced seller" at a point where the value of the investment was lower than the original purchase price, becoming a real cost. As a result, the council's £1m investment in UBS multi asset income fund suffered a £0.247m loss in value when the fund closed on 24 September, which is charged as a one-off cost to the general fund revenue budget

findings.paper_title: 11. TM Outturn report 2024-25 and 2025-26 Q1 update
findings.headline: Commercial tenant loss eliminated investment returns in 2024/25
findings.detail: Commercial investments were forecast to yield £0.4m but actually yielded 0% due to major tenant loss. Further deterioration is forecast for 2025/26 with £0.3m negative returns expected, requiring reserve draws to prevent revenue impact.
findings.matters: Tenant loss and zero yields indicate commercial property asset quality issues; dependency on smoothing reserves to cover losses signals mounting revenue pressure
findings.quote: The investments actually provided an annual yield of 0% in 2024/25 after a contribution from a smoothing reserve of £0.002m to smooth annual fluctuations on the council's revenue budget. This was primarily down to the loss of a major tenant.

findings.paper_title: 09 Cabinet - Sept 2025 - Budget Monitor Month 3 v3
findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan shows £10m+ budget gap over the next two years, with no sustainable funding solution identified.
findings.detail: The council set a balanced budget for 2025/26 but the MTFP forecast a £10m gap over the following two years, with £12m required for 2026/27 alone. The document states 'the ongoing viability into future years is intrinsically linked to these discussions' and notes that in-year pressures are likely to increase the gap further. No sustainable funding solution has been identified.
findings.matters: This shows the council's budget is balanced only through one-off measures and savings plans that may not hold up. The medium-term outlook is deteriorating, not improving.
findings.figures: £10m gap over two years; £12m required for 2026/27 alone
findings.quote: The table below shows that in February 2025 the council set a balanced budget for 2025/26 and forecast that it would have a budget gap of £10m over the following two years, with £12m being required for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 09 Cabinet - Sept 2025 - Budget Monitor Month 3 v3
findings.headline: Capital scheme funding gap: Birnbeck Pier project has lost £5.25m RNLI contribution and council cannot find replacement funding.
findings.detail: The Birnbeck Pier repair project, which is part of joint place-making initiatives, was being funded with a £5.25m contribution from the RNLI. The RNLI has withdrawn this funding. The council states 'Given the council's financial challenges described above, it is not possible to identify further funding to cover the RNLI funding shortfall' and a further report is due to Council in September.
findings.matters: This demonstrates that the council's financial pressures are now constraining its ability to fund major capital projects, even where external funding is involved. It shows capital ambitions may need to be scaled back.
findings.figures: £5.25m RNLI funding withdrawn; no replacement funding available
findings.quote: At the time of writing this report the future of the project remains uncertain following the decision by the RNLI to remove the £5.25m of planned funding towards the pier repair costs part of the project. Given the council's financial challenges described above, it is not possible to identify further funding to cover the RNLI funding shortfall.

findings.paper_title: 09 Cabinet - Sept 2025 - Budget Monitor Month 3 v3
findings.headline: Recycling income forecast is £589k below budget and identified as an ongoing risk for further deterioration.
findings.detail: The waste service is receiving £589k less income than budgeted because the recycling materials market remains 'less buoyant than in recent years'. Despite collecting more recycling materials following changes to kerbside collections, the lower commodity prices mean lower revenue. The service has identified this as a key risk for deterioration over the coming months.
findings.matters: This is a structural market issue, not a temporary variance. It suggests income budgets based on historical commodity prices are now optimistic and could worsen further if markets decline.
findings.figures: £589k income shortfall; described as key risk for further deterioration
findings.quote: The recycling materials market remains less buoyant than in recent years which means that although the council is now collecting more recycling materials following the changes to kerbside collections, it will receive £589k less income compared to the budget. The service has identified this as a key risk for further deterioration during the year and will continue to monitor closely in the coming months.

findings.paper_title: 09 Cabinet - Sept 2025 - Budget Monitor Month 3 v3
findings.headline: Council faces potential Section 114 notice if unable to balance budget, which would restrict spending to statutory services only.
findings.detail: The document explicitly discusses the Chief Finance Officer's powers under Section 114 of the Local Government Finance Act 1988 to issue a notice if the council is unable to deliver a balanced budget. If issued, no new expenditure would be permitted except for funding statutory services including safeguarding vulnerable people. The document states the council is 'wanting to avoid issuing a S114 notice' but senior leaders are 'acutely aware of these responsibilities'.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a formal declaration of financial emergency. It would severely restrict the council's operations and signal to lenders that the authority has lost financial control.
findings.figures: No specific figures; the mechanism is that S114 would restrict all discretionary spending
findings.quote: Should expenditure continue to exceed the council's available resources after exploring these options the Chief Finance Officer has the responsibility under S114 of the local government finance act 1988 to legally suspend spending for a period of time if they judge the council is unable to deliver a balanced budget or the imminent prospect of securing one in the future.

findings.paper_title: 09 Cabinet - Sept 2025 - Budget Monitor Month 3 v3
findings.headline: Only 87% of the £20m+ savings plan is forecast to be delivered, with some high-risk areas falling short.
findings.detail: The council identified £20m+ of savings needed to balance 2025/26, but the forecast shows only £17.5m (87%) will be achieved. The leisure contract transformation saving of £350k has slipped to near year-end and will deliver only £251k shortfall this year. Other areas including childrens' sufficiency transformation (designed to save £0.364m) won't achieve savings until 2026/27.
findings.matters: Savings plans are falling short at Month 3, with some key transformation projects delayed. This suggests savings targets are optimistic and the council may need to find additional mitigations or accept further overspend.
findings.figures: £17.5m delivered of £20m+ target (87%); £251k shortfall on leisure contract; £0.364m sufficiency savings deferred to 2026/27
findings.quote: The summary indicates that £17.5m, or 87% of the savings will be achieved by the year-end and reflects the detailed work carried out to validate these plans before they were included within the budget.

findings.paper_title: 09 Cabinet - Sept 2025 - Budget Monitor Month 3 v3
findings.headline: Council is drawing down £9.2m of one-off reserves for 2025/26 and this is described as a temporary measure pending a sustainable solution.
findings.detail: As part of the MTFP for 2025-2028, the council approved using £9.2m of reserves for 2025/26 as a temporary measure to balance the budget. Additionally, 95% of the contingency budget (£1.678m) is being released to fund in-year pressures. These one-off measures indicate the council cannot balance the budget from recurrent revenue and must erode reserves.
findings.matters: Reserves are being used as a gap-filler rather than for genuine contingencies. If demand or funding pressures worsen, the council will have little buffer and may need to issue a Section 114 notice.
findings.figures: £9.2m of reserves for 2025/26 only; £1.678m contingency being released (95% of total)
findings.quote: Council also approved using £9.2m of one-off reserves for 2025/26 as a short-term measure until a more sustainable funding solution to permanently close the gap could be identified in later years.

findings.paper_title: 09 Cabinet - Sept 2025 - Budget Monitor Month 3 v3
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Budget deficit forecast to reach £46m by year-end, with statutory override expiring in March 2029.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit, which was over £26m at the start of the year, is forecast to reach £46m by year-end (overspend of £21m partially offset by Safety Valve grant of £1m). This is being held off-balance-sheet under a temporary statutory override which expires March 2029. The council's general fund reserve is only £10.4m, insufficient to cover this deficit if the override ends without amendment.
findings.matters: This represents a contingent liability of £46m that could hit the revenue budget in March 2029 unless government extends the override or provides alternative funding. It represents over four times the council's total general reserves.
findings.figures: Deficit forecast £46m by year-end (was £26m at start); general reserve £10.4m; override expires March 2029
findings.quote: The council's DSG deficit was over £26m at the beginning of the year and is likely to reach £46m by the end of the year; the council's general reserve balance is currently only £10.4m which means that it would not be sufficient to fund the deficit in its entirety should the statutory over-ride not be in place.

findings.paper_title: 09 Cabinet - Sept 2025 - Budget Monitor Month 3 v3
findings.headline: Government consultation proposes cutting North Somerset's core funding by nearly 20% from as early as 2026/27.
findings.detail: The government's Fair Funding Review 2.0 consultation proposes fundamental reforms to local authority funding with implementation potentially from 2026/27. Technical analysis by external experts shows North Somerset would lose £17.4m (19.8% of current funding) under the proposals. North Somerset council tax is £1,794 per head vs a notional £2,000 assumed in the formula, putting it at a significant disadvantage.
findings.matters: This is not a future risk but a confirmed government proposal being consulted on. A 20% cut to core funding would make the council's current budget position unsustainable and would require either major service cuts, significant council tax rises, or both.
findings.figures: £17.4m reduction (19.8% of current funding); council tax £1,794 vs notional £2,000; implementation possibly 2026/27
findings.quote: An earlier review of the consultation data shows that the government proposals will reduce the core funding to residents of North Somerset by nearly 20%, and importantly, even though we have not been provided with any agreed values, the planned reduction in funding will be implemented as soon as 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 09 Cabinet - Sept 2025 - Budget Monitor Month 3 v3
findings.headline: Adults social care has a £1.6m shortfall on income-based savings.
findings.detail: The council was relying on £3.1m of savings from S117 recommissioning arrangements with the Integrated Care Board, but the forecast now shows only £1.5m will be delivered, leaving a £1.6m shortfall. This is a structural income problem, not a one-off timing issue.
findings.matters: A major saving plan is failing to materialise. If the council cannot recover this income from the ICB, it will need to identify alternative savings or accept the overspend.
findings.figures: £1.6m shortfall on a planned £3.1m saving; only £1.5m forecast to be achieved
findings.quote: One area of concern relates to the income received through S117 recommissioning arrangements with the Integrated Care Board. The forecast indicates that only £1.5m of the £3.1m saving will be achieved resulting in a shortfall of £1.6m for the year.

findings.paper_title: 09 Cabinet - Sept 2025 - Budget Monitor Month 3 v3
findings.headline: Children's social care demand continues to exceed budget despite a £14m+ re-base in February.
findings.detail: The children's services budget was re-based upwards by over £14m in February 2025 to cover expected care placements and inflation, but the forecast is already £4.998m (9.73%) over that revised budget. Ten additional children have been brought into care since the budget was set (six in Feb-Mar, four in Apr-Jun), costing £3.6m alone. Residential placements are being used more because of insufficient local foster care capacity.
findings.matters: The council is unable to forecast or control demand for statutory children's social care despite attempting to re-base budgets, suggesting an ongoing structural problem that could worsen.
findings.figures: £4.998m overspend on a budget of £51.361m; ten additional children brought into care; £3.6m cost impact from just the new placements
findings.quote: the number of children in care within North Somerset has risen sharply in recent years, and instead of stabilising, this trend has continued over recent months. The council is continuing to experience sufficiency issues which means that some of the children being brought into care are being placed into residential settings rather than be able to go to an in-house or independent foster carer, with some of these placements being out of area

findings.paper_title: 09 Cabinet - Sept 2025 - Budget Monitor Month 3 v3
findings.headline: Revenue budget forecast £4.495m overspent despite planned mitigations.
findings.detail: The council approved a budget of £245.357m but is forecasting spend of £249.852m (1.83% overspend). Services are forecast to overspend by £11.443m, partially offset by £6.949m in savings and mitigations from non-service budgets. The mitigations include one-off items like releasing contingency (95% of £1.678m) and deferring borrowing costs (£986k), which are not sustainable.
findings.matters: The council is relying on one-off mitigations to balance the budget in-year, leaving no buffer for further pressures and raising questions about financial sustainability in future years.
findings.figures: £4.495m overspend, £11.443m service pressures, £6.949m mitigations
findings.quote: Managers forecast that the council will spend £249.852m during the year to deliver services to the public, Unfortunately, this is £4.495m more than the council has available to spend, which would be a variance of £1.83%, assuming no further action is taken to balance the budget.

findings.paper_title: 13 Corporate Services and S151 restructure
findings.headline: Restructure costs (£31,600 in 2025/26, £128,300 in 2026/27) to be covered by unspecified future savings programs
findings.detail: The council budgets specific restructure costs but states these 'will be covered by future savings programmes which are expected to deliver multi-millions of benefits.' No specific savings programs, timelines, or targets are identified in this document.
findings.matters: A lender needs clarity on whether the council's financial plan rests on concrete, identified savings or depends on hoped-for future program delivery that has not yet been quantified or committed.
findings.figures: Restructure costs: £31,600 (2025/26), £128,300 (2026/27); future savings described as 'expected to deliver multi-millions of benefits' (unquantified)
findings.quote: cost increases will be covered by future savings programmes which are expected to deliver multi-millions of benefits

findings.paper_title: 13 Corporate Services and S151 restructure
findings.headline: Section 151 role split from Corporate Services Director with explicit mandate to develop and lead financial strategy
findings.detail: New 'Assistant Director, Finance and Data Insight (S151 Officer)' role consolidates S151 responsibilities and adds explicit accountability for developing the council's financial strategy and driving evidence-based decision-making. This creates dedicated, focused financial leadership separate from transformation work.
findings.matters: Clearer S151 focus on financial strategy and evidence-based decision-making may strengthen financial controls and planning, though success depends on execution and the transformation work delivering savings.
findings.figures: New role: Assistant Director, Finance and Data Insight (S151 Officer); includes financial strategy development, evidence-based decision-making, Internal Audit oversight
findings.quote: To develop and lead on the implementation and evaluation of the Council's financial strategy

findings.paper_title: 13 Corporate Services and S151 restructure
findings.headline: Current leadership bandwidth entirely consumed by financial challenges, with no director capacity for strategic transformation
findings.detail: The report states that 'the council's ongoing financial challenges mean that the majority of the work of the current Corporate Services Director and S151 officer has been focussed on meeting that financial challenge' and notes that under the current structure 'no single director has responsibility for transformation.' The restructure creates a dedicated transformation director role.
findings.matters: Leadership being consumed by crisis management indicates acute financial pressure and suggests the council cannot execute the strategic change CIPFA identified as necessary for survival without organizational restructuring.
findings.figures: No director currently responsible for transformation; majority of CSD and S151 capacity absorbed by financial challenges
findings.quote: the council's ongoing financial challenges mean that the majority of the work of the current Corporate Services Director and S151 officer has been focussed on meeting that financial challenge

findings.paper_title: 13 Corporate Services and S151 restructure
findings.headline: CIPFA financial resilience report identifies need to rebuild reserves and deliver complex transformation at scale for sustainability
findings.detail: The council explicitly cites CIPFA's assessment that 'the Council's future sustainability will depend on delivering complex transformation at scale, rebuilding reserves, and embedding integrated planning across services and finances' as the rationale for this restructure. This is the driving concern for the organizational change.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know an external expert has identified reserve-rebuilding as necessary for the council's future sustainability, signalling known financial position concerns.
findings.figures: CIPFA financial resilience report assessment; sustainability requires transformation at scale, rebuilding reserves, integrated planning
findings.quote: the Council's future sustainability will depend on delivering complex transformation at scale, rebuilding reserves, and embedding integrated planning across services and finances

news_drafts.paper_title: 13 Cabinet report - MTFP & Revenue Budget 2027-2030 - September 2026
